transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Okafor, thank you for meeting with me. I need to talk to you about what happened with your medication yesterday. There was a serious error. I ordered ten times the amount of anticoagulant that you should have received. Instead of five milligrams, you were given fifty.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ten times? I felt some dizziness, but I didn't realize it was a dosing error. What exactly did that do to my body?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Because the dose was so high, your blood became too thin. This led to internal bleeding in your gastrointestinal tract, which is why we had to bring in the emergency team to stabilize you and give you a reversal agent to stop the bleed. Does that make sense so far?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It makes sense, though it is quite alarming. I trust the process here, but I can't help but wonder how a ten-fold error even happens. Was it a typing mistake?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was. I typed the wrong number into the system and didn't catch it before it was processed. I'm sorry for any confusion this caused you. We were really busy on the ward yesterday and things were moving fast.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate the apology, but I'm more concerned about the fact that I almost bled out because of a typo. I spent my whole career teaching students to double-check their work. I'm feeling quite shaken by the lack of oversight.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can hear how distressing this is for you. To feel like the very people caring for you weren't paying attention to the details—especially when you value precision so much—must be incredibly unsettling.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is. It makes me question every other pill I've taken since I got here. If this happened once, what else—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Look, we just need to move forward now. The bleeding has stopped and your vitals are stable. I have to go check on another patient in a few minutes, so I want to make sure we're on the same page. Do you have any other questions about the dose itself?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do. I want to know what the long-term effects of that massive overdose are. Will this affect my kidney function or—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can tell you that right now your labs are returning to normal. It's a very scary experience, and I can see you're still processing the shock of it all. I really want to support you through this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate the empathy, but I'm still asking about my kidneys. Was there any organ damage?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's wrap this up quickly because I'm running behind. As I said, the reversal agent worked. We've corrected the coagulation levels.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're rushing me. I'm trying to understand the damage to my body. Who is going to ensure this doesn't happen again? I don't want to just "move forward" without a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand you're worried about the safety of your care. It's completely valid to feel that way after such a mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Then what is the plan? How are we fixing the system so the next person doesn't get ten times their dose?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll see what the administration says. Stay tuned for an email from the patient safety team. They usually send something out after an incident report is filed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: An email? I'm lying in a hospital bed. I want a specific protocol change. I want to know who is checking your orders.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll keep an eye on things. Just keep resting and we'll figure it out. I really have to get going now. I'll stop by later.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('move forward now', 'wrap this up quickly', 'running behind', 'have to get going now').

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the first turn, lay language was used, and comprehension was checked once ('Does that make sense so far?').

A.justification: A direct apology was offered, but it was immediately diluted by an excuse regarding being busy on the ward.

R.justification: Resident named specific emotions ('distressing', 'unsettling', 'scary experience', 'shock') and referenced the patient's specific value of precision.

T.justification: The resident provided only placeholders and vague responses ('We'll see what the administration says', 'stay tuned', 'we'll figure it out').
